227.t: The Americanization of Emily and the start of songwriting
227.s: After vocal albums and the Andy Williams show, Mandel got a Filmways picture that let him write his first song of consequence.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: And really… then did the Andy Williams, I was gonna say Andy Warhol, Andy Williams and right after the Andy Williams thing, I really got connected up with Filmways [Production Company] and got a shot to do The Americanization of Emily, a very good picture, a

227.t: How The Shadow of Your Smile became a song
227.s: Mandel says the Sandpiper theme was demoed on piano before scoring and then turned into a song.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: After I'd done it. Actually we had decided before that. I had the song in piano form and demoed it, ‘cause they wanted to hear the theme before I ever put it to score, and that was when we decided to make a song out of it.

227.t: The Shining Sea and Peggy Lee's lyric
227.s: Mandel tells how Peggy Lee wrote a lyric that matched the screen action of The Russians Are Coming without knowing the scene.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: Right, that was done after the movie, we realized we had something that could be a song and Peggy Lee did an amazing thing, to me. She is a very intuitive lady, but I gave her this theme and I asked her, “Would you like to write a lyric to it?” And she said, “Yes,” and she wrote it and it was…

227.s: Mandel tells how Altman's lyric, written by his teenage son, and a Leonard Cohen temp track led him to write Suicide Is Painless after some stiff drinks, and the lesson never to throw anything away.
227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: You remember the Last Supper scene, when, “The Painless Pole” [Polish], the dentist in the outfit was going to commit suicide because he had not been able to get it up with a W.A.C. [Women’s Army Corp] the night before and he was afraid his ladies man reputation in the outfit was totally down the…

227.s: Mandel says Quietly There was source music in Harper, with a later lyric by Morgan Ames, with whom he also wrote Unless It's You.
227.q: Yeah, yeah. I didn’t really write it for, Harper, it’s just something that I came up with and I put it into, Harper, as a piece of source music but it wasn't really written for that movie.

227.s: Mandel explains Emily began as a motif for the Julie Andrews character, and remembers admiring Gene Puerling, with whom he worked on the Manhattan Transfer album.
227.q: Right, it started with a motif that I thought fitted the character that Julie Andrews played. You know [sings Emily, Emily] I wanted to get kind of a sort of a purity in a nice ethereal way, type of feeling, it seemed to capsulize what she was to me at that time. And the song just kind of spun…

227.t: Sure as You're Born and the Bergmans
227.s: Mandel recalls Alan and Marilyn Bergman writing a lyric for the Harper theme, praising their professionalism.
227.q: “Sure as You're Born,” came to be called, “Sure as You're Born,” it was originally the main title theme from, Harper and it didn't stay that way very long because before the picture was released Alan Bergman came up with a lyric. The Warner Brothers called them and had – I’d never met them before,…

227.t: Where Do You Start? and a playwright's lyric
227.s: Mandel describes how a playwright's divorce lyric inspired his music, which the Bergmans then matched with the same subject without knowing.
227.q: “Where Do You Start?” had a very interesting, that had a very interesting genealogy. A well-known playwright, who will remain unnamed, liked to write lyrics and one of them came my way and strangely enough this is another one of those things like the Peggy Lee story. He wrote a lyric about a…

227.t: I Wish I'd Met You and Richard Rodney Bennett
227.s: Mandel describes writing music to a lyric by Richard Rodney Bennett and Frank Underwood, and why he likes setting finished lyrics.
227.q: I wrote that totally to a lyric, Richard Rodney Bennett sent me a lyric he had written, you know Richard Rodney Bennett’s a rather famous composer in his own right and a wonderful film composer. He had written, you know, Equus, also for Sidney Lumet, Far From the Madding Crowd…

227.t: Cinnamon and Clove, I Never Told You and Lena Horne's song
227.s: Mandel tells the origins of Cinnamon and Clove, I Never Told You from That Cold Day in the Park, and a recent song for Lena Horne.
227.q: “Cinnamon and Clove,” I’d just come back from Brazil and wanted to write in that idiom and that's what I wrote. And gave it to Alan and Marilyn and they just came up with, “Cinnamon and Clove,” which actually came from a Jorge Amado novel, a Brazilian, really great Brazilian novelist – a Brazilian…

227.t: You Are There and Dave Frishberg
227.s: Mandel says You Are There came to him one morning in the car and Dave Frishberg wrote the lyric after several attempts.
227.q: “You Are There,” is just one of those songs that emerged one morning, I was on my way to an appointment and I stopped the car and wrote it down, it all came out in one – it’s the kind of a song that you’d never set out to write and I didn’t know what to do with that song, I had five different…

227.t: The Manhattan Transfer Christmas album and Mandel's Christmas song
227.s: Mandel describes working with Manhattan Transfer and his song that came out sounding like Christmas, which the Bergmans confirmed.
227.q: I said for some reason this sounds like Christmas, I don’t know what makes a song sound like Christmas, I probably wrote it in July or something and took it to the Bergman’s and they said, “Yeah, that sounds like a Christmas song.” And then Marilyn said, “What makes it sound like a Christmas song?”…

10.t: Plan to publish Joplin rags and the songs Why and If You Knew
10.s: Carew proposed Morton play and publish Joplin rags, but Morton preferred songs; Carew wrote words for Why and If You Knew.
10.q: that the thing that would help him would be to take Joplin rags and play them in his style, and then publish those. Because I'm, I'm, uh, 60 or 70 years behind time in this music business, and sheet music is a lot to me, you see? Mm-hmm. although I didn't realize that. So I broached it to him, and…

176.t: Coconut Island and the Coconut Grove theme song
176.s: Billie explains how Coconut Island became her theme song at the Coconut Grove.
176.q: Well, when I played that Coconut Island, that was when I was working with the pig pig, but they named me the Coconut Grove. So why they named me the Coconut Grove, that's why I played that Coconut Island. I changed that theme song, see, to the Coconut Grove, see.

434.t: Gus Bivona and the tune 'Baby What You Did'
434.s: After a musical excerpt, Allen recalls meeting clarinetist Gus Bivona when he moved to Van Nuys and how the tune got its title.
434.q: I was at a house I’d lived in for a few years in Van Nuys I think it was, a subsection of Los Angeles. I had an inferior piano. I don’t know how I acquired that but it was an old upright. But the fellow you hear playing the clarinet, a very good clarinetist and marvelous guy named Gus Bivona, who…

974.t: How he began writing songs and performing them himself
974.s: He wrote limericks in high school and later songs including a 1973-74 gas shortage song, and always planned to perform his own songs, including an upcoming off-Broadway show.
974.q: Well I wrote poetry in high school as a sort of a way to communicate to friends and have fun. And I found out I could write a limerick pretty easy, it’s not that hard to do, the English language does have some rhymes in it, and if you think about it you can find them. Then in the 30s, all of a…

1047.s: She explains the melodic arc as repeated attempts at a relationship ending in acceptance of truth.

And the arc tells a story. So in the very beginning there are those three lines, right? And what happened for me is that I…

460.t: Land of Passion and writing lyrics
460.s: Laws describes Land of Passion, its Grammy nomination, his duets with Johnny and Debra, and lyrics as the title poem.
460.q: Land of Passion. As a matter of fact, it got a Grammy nomination, that track. Let’s see. All three of those up there, they were Grammy nominated. That’s what those plaques are for. I think one is In the Beginning, I think one is Land of Passion, and I can’t remember the other one. Yeah, I started…

136.t: Japanese song titles on the LP
136.s: Brown asks about 'Soshu no yoru' and 'Kyoshu'; she explains the titles.
136.ch: Boston, Berklee and New York encounters
136.q: “Soshū no yoru” is a Japanese pop tune [composed by Saijō Yaso and Niki Kitao]. Pop music. “Soshū” is the name of a place in China [Sūzhōu]. Yoru is “evening,” as you know. “Evening of Soshū,” that‟s how it‟s supposed to be.
